SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as previous waves, many Americans exhibit short fuses -- and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. notes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for not assimilating. They have convinced themselves that, instead of adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals -- most of whom come from Asia or Latin America -- expect the rest of us to accommodate them. They go ballistic over little things -- Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries that offer bilingual story time, or having to "press one for English." Yet, even as they look down on new immigrants, many Americans look back fondly upon their immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy or Poland, he jumped off the boat, immediately draped himself in the American flag, ripped out his native tongue, and abandoned his culture -- all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy." Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese. The Irish did not settle in Boston and join organizations like the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture. And even while Americans complain about how the current crop of immigrants aren't like their predecessors, they miss the irony: At the time, there were people who said the same thing about their ancestors; the Germans were thought to not be like the English, the Irish weren't like the Germans, the Italians weren't like the Irish etc. And the Chinese weren't like anyone who had come before them, and so they were labeled "unassimilable" by the Tom Tancredos of that era. Some things never change. When I was growing up in Central California, which is home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia, thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would do a feature. And, in the days that followed, someone would write an angry letter to the editor complaining that these people weren't melting into the pot. Yet, there is more melting going on than one might think, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three kinds of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, etc.); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, etc.); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, etc.). Far from discovering that recent immigrants are ducking the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival." Of course, individual groups still fall behind in some categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants have low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants have low levels of economic assimilation. And Canadian and Indian immigrants have low levels of civic assimilation, since few of them become citizens. But, overall, the news is good. After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group tried to resist the process, they wouldn't stand a chance. Assimilation happens, whether the immigrants are ready or not. Those are the facts. Of course, fear doesn't listen to facts. That is something else that hasn't changed. Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as previous waves did, many Americans display short fuses -- and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. observes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for failing to assimilate.

Many have convinced themselves that, rather than adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals -- most of whom come from Asia or Latin America -- expect the rest of us to accommodate them. They grow indignant over the smallest things: Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries that offer bilingual story time, or having to "press one for English."

Yet, even as they look down upon new immigrants, many Americans reflect fondly upon their own immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy, or Poland, he leaped off the boat, immediately draped himself in the American flag, cast off his native tongue, and abandoned his culture -- all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy."

But the Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese, did they? Nor did the Irish settle in Boston and join organizations such as the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture. And even as Americans lament how the current crop of immigrants differs from their predecessors, they overlook the irony: in their own time, those very predecessors were the subject of identical complaints. The Germans were thought to be unlike the English, the Irish unlike the Germans, the Italians unlike the Irish, and so on. The Chinese, meanwhile, were deemed unlike anyone who had come before them, and thus were branded "unassimilable" by the Tom Tancredos of that era.

Some things never change. When I was growing up in Central California -- home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia -- thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would run a feature on the occasion, and, in the days that followed, someone would invariably write an angry letter to the editor, complaining that these people were not melting into the pot.

Yet there is far more melting under way than one might suppose, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three forms of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, and the like); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, and so forth); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, and more).

Far from discovering that recent immigrants are evading the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival."

To be sure, individual groups still lag in certain categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants exhibit low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants show low levels of economic assimilation. And Canadian and Indian immigrants demonstrate low levels of civic assimilation, since few of them become citizens. Overall, however, the news is encouraging.

After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group set out to resist the process, it would not stand a chance. Assimilation happens, whether immigrants are ready for it or not.

Those are the facts. Fear, of course, does not listen to facts. And that, too, is something that has not changed.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- When it comes to debating whether today's newcomers blend into American society as fast as earlier generations did, plenty of Americans show little patience -- and even less recollection of the past. As Ruben Navarrette Jr. points out, immigrants have faced accusations of failing to assimilate for as long as this nation has existed. Many people have persuaded themselves that today's arrivals -- the majority hailing from Asia or Latin America -- refuse to embrace American ways and instead demand that everyone else bend to suit them. The smallest things set them off: Mexican flags, taco vendors, libraries hosting story hours in two languages, or being told to "press one for English."

Curiously, while these same Americans sneer at newcomers, they wax nostalgic about their own immigrant forebears. According to family folklore, the moment grandpa stepped off the boat from Ireland, Germany, Italy, or Poland, he wrapped himself in the Stars and Stripes, cast aside his mother tongue, forgot his heritage, and burst into a chorus of "Yankee Doodle Dandy." But the Germans who settled in Milwaukee didn't just start brewing beer and making cheese by accident. The Irish who put down roots in Boston didn't avoid founding groups like the Hibernian Society to protect their traditions and identity.

And here's the irony that escapes those who grumble that modern immigrants don't measure up to earlier ones: back then, people said precisely the same thing about their ancestors. The Germans supposedly weren't like the English, the Irish weren't like the Germans, the Italians weren't like the Irish, and on it went. The Chinese, meanwhile, weren't like anybody who had preceded them, which earned them the "unassimilable" label from the equivalent of Tom Tancredo in those days. Some patterns simply repeat themselves.

Growing up in Central California, a region with a substantial community of immigrants from Southeast Asia, I remember thousands of people coming together to mark Hmong New Year. The local paper would run a story about it. Predictably, within days, some reader would fire off an indignant letter to the editor grumbling that these folks refused to blend into the melting pot.

Yet a fresh report from the Manhattan Institute suggests far more blending is occurring than critics assume. Described as the inaugural annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the analysis was authored by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It examined three types of integration: economic, covering jobs, schooling, homeownership and similar factors; cultural, including marrying outside one's group, English ability, and family size; and civic, such as gaining citizenship, serving in the armed forces, and taking part in politics.

Rather than confirming that today's immigrants are dodging assimilation, the report determined that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival."

Naturally, some groups still trail in particular areas. Immigrants from China and India show weak cultural assimilation. Those from Mexico rank low on economic measures. And immigrants from Canada and India score poorly on civic integration, largely because so few pursue citizenship. Still, the overall picture is encouraging. More than two centuries in, America remains remarkably good at absorbing its newcomers. Even a group determined to fight the process would have no real hope of succeeding. Assimilation takes place regardless of whether immigrants welcome it.

Those are the facts. Then again, fear pays no attention to facts -- and that, too, is nothing new.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. serves on the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and writes a nationally syndicated column. Read his column here. The views expressed in this commentary belong exclusively to the author.

# The Myth of Effortless Assimilation

Many Americans today criticize recent immigrants for failing to assimilate quickly enough. A common complaint is that newcomers cling to their native languages, traditions, and customs, expecting the broader society to accommodate them rather than making the effort to adapt to American ways of life. This frustration reflects a widely held belief that immigrants should shed their old identities and embrace American culture as rapidly as possible.

Underlying this criticism is a romanticized vision of America's own immigrant past. Many Americans idealize their ancestors, imagining that these earlier arrivals abandoned their native cultures the moment they set foot on American soil and immediately embraced a wholehearted American identity. According to this comforting narrative, previous generations of immigrants assimilated smoothly and completely, unlike the newcomers of today.

The historical record, however, tells a very different story. Immigrant groups such as the Germans, Irish, and Italians did not simply cast aside their heritage upon arrival. Instead, they actively preserved their cultural identities through a rich network of ethnic organizations, mutual aid societies, religious institutions, foreign-language newspapers, and community traditions. Rather than fully assimilating, these groups maintained strong ties to their roots for generations, building enclaves where their languages and customs continued to thrive.

What emerges from this history is a repeating pattern of prejudice. Each successive wave of immigrants has been criticized by those who came before as somehow fundamentally different and "unassimilable." The very groups once condemned as incapable of becoming truly American eventually came to be seen as part of the mainstream—only to level the same accusations against those who followed them. This cycle reveals that the anxiety over assimilation is less about the immigrants themselves and more about a recurring bias that resurfaces with each new group.

The author illustrates this ongoing pattern through his own experience with Hmong immigrants in Central California. When members of the Hmong community held their cultural celebrations, local residents responded with complaints—echoing the very same objections that had been raised against earlier immigrant groups throughout American history. In this way, the Hmong experience serves as a contemporary example of a prejudice that has been repeated again and again, demonstrating that today's criticisms are simply the latest chapter in a long and familiar story.

# The Recurring Myth of the "Unassimilable" Immigrant

A common refrain echoes throughout contemporary American political discourse: today's immigrants, particularly those arriving from Asia and Latin America, are somehow different from those who came before. Critics argue that these newcomers cling stubbornly to their native languages, cluster together in ethnic enclaves, and resist adopting American customs and values. Unlike the immigrants of generations past, the argument goes, these modern arrivals refuse to become "truly American," threatening the cultural cohesion that has long defined the nation. This perception has fueled anxiety and political tension, shaping debates over immigration policy and national identity.

Ruben Navarrette Jr. challenges this widely held assumption by turning to the historical record. Rather than accepting the premise that current immigrants represent a novel and troubling departure from tradition, Navarrette examines how earlier waves of newcomers were received upon their arrival. What he discovers is a striking and instructive pattern—one that undermines the notion that today's concerns are new or unique.

## History Repeats Itself

Navarrette points out that virtually every major immigrant group in American history faced the very same accusations now leveled against Asians and Latinos. When German immigrants arrived, they were criticized for maintaining their own language, publishing German-language newspapers, and preserving their distinct communities. The Irish were viewed with suspicion and hostility, their Catholic faith and cultural practices seen as fundamentally incompatible with American life. Italian immigrants encountered similar disdain, dismissed as unable or unwilling to shed their Old World traditions. Chinese immigrants, too, were branded as perpetual foreigners—so allegedly "unassimilable" that they became the target of exclusionary laws designed to keep them out entirely.

In each case, the established population insisted that these particular newcomers were incapable of becoming genuinely American. And in each case, that judgment proved to be shortsighted.

## The Irony of Assimilation

The deeper irony Navarrette identifies lies in the fact that these earlier groups did preserve significant elements of their cultures—and yet they still became woven into the fabric of American society. German, Irish, and Italian traditions have long since blended into the broader national culture, celebrated today rather than feared. The very groups once condemned as threats to American identity are now regarded as quintessentially American. What was once seen as dangerous separatism came to be understood, in retrospect, as a normal and even enriching part of the immigrant experience.

This historical perspective reveals that the complaints voiced against today's immigrants are not the product of any genuinely new phenomenon. Instead, they represent a recurring cycle—an anxiety that resurfaces with each successive wave of newcomers, only to be proven unfounded as those immigrants and their descendants integrate over time. The accusation of being "unassimilable" says less about the immigrants themselves than about the fears of those who receive them.

## Conclusion

By placing current immigration debates within their proper historical context, Navarrette exposes the flawed logic behind the claim that Asian and Latin American immigrants are uniquely resistant to assimilation. The pattern is unmistakable: each generation of Americans has looked upon the latest arrivals with suspicion, forgetting that their own ancestors were once viewed the same way. Recognizing this cycle allows us to approach today's immigration debates with greater perspective and humility—understanding that what feels like an unprecedented crisis is, in truth, a familiar chapter in a long and repeating American story.

# Today's Immigrants Are Assimilating Just Fine — History Proves It

**By Ruben Navarrette Jr.**

SAN DIEGO — Every generation of Americans seems to convince itself of the same comforting lie: that the immigrants who came before were the good ones — hardworking, patriotic, eager to learn English and become American — while the immigrants arriving today are somehow different, resistant to the melting pot, unwilling to blend in.

I've heard this song my whole life. As the grandson of a Mexican immigrant who crossed into this country as a boy, I've watched politicians and pundits wring their hands over whether "these people" will ever truly become American. And every time, I want to hand them a history book.

Because here's the inconvenient truth: The anxiety about assimilation isn't new. It's practically a national tradition.

## We've Always Panicked About the Newcomers

Consider Benjamin Franklin, one of our Founding Fathers, who in 1751 fretted about German immigrants pouring into Pennsylvania. He worried they would never adopt English customs, that they clung to their own language, and that they would "Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them." Sound familiar? Swap out "German" for "Mexican" or "Guatemalan," and you could drop that quote into a cable news segment tonight.

The Germans, of course, assimilated. So did the Irish, who in the 19th century were caricatured as drunken, disloyal Catholics who could never be trusted to embrace American democracy. So did the Italians, the Poles, the Jews from Eastern Europe — all of whom were told, in their day, that they were too foreign, too clannish, too different to ever really fit in.

They fit in. Their grandchildren became doctors, soldiers, teachers, and yes, opinion columnists. The panic was always wrong. And it's wrong again today.

## What the Data Actually Says

Don't just take my word for it. Take the word of the Manhattan Institute, a right-leaning think tank not exactly known for cheerleading immigration.

In its landmark study, the Index of Immigrant Assimilation, authored by economist Jacob Vigdor, the Manhattan Institute measured how thoroughly immigrants blend into American society across economic, cultural, and civic dimensions. The findings should embarrass the doom-sayers.

Vigdor found that today's immigrants are, in fact, assimilating — and in some respects doing so *more* rapidly than immigrants of the past. The children of immigrants overwhelmingly speak English. By the second generation, English fluency is nearly universal, and by the third, ancestral languages have largely faded — the same pattern followed by the Germans and Italians before them.

The study did note that some groups, particularly Mexican immigrants, show slower economic and civic assimilation. But Vigdor was clear about the reason: legal status, not cultural stubbornness. Undocumented immigrants can't naturalize, can't fully integrate into the formal economy, and remain stuck in a legal limbo that has nothing to do with their desire to become American. Fix the immigration system, and you remove the very barriers that slow assimilation.

In other words, the problem isn't the immigrants. It's the broken laws we've saddled them with.

## The Melting Pot Still Works

Walk through any immigrant neighborhood in America today and you'll see the same story my family lived. The first generation works backbreaking jobs and speaks the old language at home. The second generation grows up bilingual, cheering for American football teams and dreaming American dreams. The third generation often can't order a meal in their grandparents' native tongue.

This is assimilation in motion. It's messy, it takes a generation or two, and it has always looked exactly this way.

Latinos are enlisting in the military, starting businesses at higher rates than the general population, buying homes, and intermarrying across ethnic lines. Intermarriage — perhaps the ultimate measure of assimilation — continues to climb. You don't marry into a society you're refusing to join.

## The Real Lesson of History

The story of American immigration is a story of anxiety followed by amnesia. Each wave of newcomers is treated as a threat, and then, a generation later, celebrated as the "good" immigrants who did it the "right way" — usually as a cudgel against whoever is arriving next.

We should have learned by now. The melting pot isn't broken. It never was. It just requires the one ingredient Americans have always been reluctant to offer: patience, and a little faith that this generation of strivers will do exactly what every previous one did.

They'll become us. They already are.

*Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a syndicated columnist and a member of the USA Today Board of Contributors. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own.*

# The Myth of the Melting Pot: How We Forgot Our Own Immigrant History

There's a story Americans love to tell ourselves. It goes like this: earlier immigrants—the Italians, the Irish, the Poles, the Germans, the Jews—came to America, embraced English, discarded their old-world ways, and assimilated seamlessly into the great American melting pot. Today's immigrants, the story continues, are different. They cling to their languages, live in ethnic enclaves, and refuse to become "real" Americans.

It's a compelling narrative. It's also almost entirely false.

## What History Actually Shows

The historical record tells a very different story from our sanitized collective memory. Consider language. German-language newspapers flourished in America well into the 20th century—by 1900, there were nearly 800 German-language publications in the United States. Entire regions of the Midwest conducted daily life primarily in German, with German-language schools, churches, and businesses. Cincinnati and Milwaukee had public schools offering instruction in German for decades.

The Italians who arrived in the late 19th and early 20th centuries clustered in "Little Italys" where they could go weeks without speaking English. Many first-generation immigrants never learned the language at all, relying on their children as intermediaries with the broader world. Polish, Yiddish, Norwegian, and Chinese communities did precisely the same.

These weren't anomalies. They were the norm.

## The Enclaves We Now Romanticize

The very ethnic neighborhoods that Americans now celebrate as charming cultural heritage sites—Chinatown, Little Italy, the old Jewish Lower East Side—were once viewed with the same suspicion and hostility directed at immigrant communities today.

Benjamin Franklin worried that German immigrants would "Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them," complaining that they refused to learn English and would never adopt American customs. Sound familiar? This anxiety about newcomers refusing to assimilate is as old as the country itself.

Catholic immigrants faced accusations that their loyalty belonged to the Pope rather than America. Chinese immigrants were deemed so fundamentally unassimilable that Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. Southern and Eastern Europeans were considered racially inferior stock who would dilute the nation's character.

Every single group we now consider unremarkably "American" was once the frightening foreign menace.

## Assimilation Takes Generations—It Always Has

Here's the crucial truth our national mythology obscures: assimilation was never quick, and it was never complete in a single generation. It happened over the course of two, three, or four generations. The immigrant's grandchildren became fully fluent, fully integrated Americans—not the immigrants themselves.

This is exactly the pattern we see with today's immigrants. Study after study confirms that the children of modern immigrants overwhelmingly speak English, and their grandchildren often speak nothing else. Second and third-generation Latino Americans follow the same linguistic trajectory as the descendants of Italian and Polish immigrants a century ago. The timeline hasn't changed. Our memory of it has.

## The Irony We Can't See

And here lies the deep irony. Many of the Americans most vocally critical of today's immigrants for "not assimilating" are themselves the descendants of immigrants who did the very things they now condemn.

The person complaining that immigrants should "learn English and speak it" may well be the great-grandchild of someone who died having never spoken a word of it. The family that celebrates its Irish or Italian heritage each year—with festivals, foods, and phrases from the old country—is expressing the exact kind of cultural retention they criticize in others.

We have selectively remembered our own history. We've transformed our ancestors' gradual, multigenerational, incomplete assimilation into an instantaneous conversion, then held new immigrants to a standard our own families never met.

## What This Should Teach Us

None of this is to say that integration doesn't matter or that shared civic bonds are unimportant. It's to say that the process works—and it always has—when we let it unfold naturally rather than demanding an overnight transformation that never actually happened in our own past.

The immigrants building lives in America today are following the same path our forebears walked. They're working, raising children who will grow up American, and gradually weaving their threads into the national fabric, just as generations did before them.

Before we complain that modern immigrants aren't assimilating fast enough, we might do well to remember our own family histories more honestly. The melting pot never melted as quickly as we like to imagine. It simmered slowly, over generations—and it produced the America we know today.

The newcomers we worry about now will, in time, become the ancestors that future Americans proudly celebrate. That's not a departure from our national story. That *is* our national story.

# The Assimilation Anxiety That Never Learns

Every generation of Americans seems convinced that *this* wave of immigrants—unlike all the ones before—will refuse to become truly American. The evidence supposedly surrounds us: the phone menus that ask us to "press one for English," the taco trucks parked on suburban corners, the cultural festivals that fill community centers with unfamiliar music. To the anxious observer, these are symptoms of a nation fragmenting into isolated enclaves. But this reading gets the story almost perfectly backward.

Consider the Hmong New Year celebrations that now anchor communities from St. Paul to Fresno. When Hmong refugees arrived after the Vietnam War, few Americans expected them to integrate easily—they came from a preliterate agricultural society, carrying trauma and customs that seemed impossibly distant from Midwestern life. Yet walk into a Hmong New Year festival today and you'll find something revealing: elders in traditional dress standing beside grandchildren in college hoodies, ball-tossing courtship rituals happening alongside conversations about the SAT. The celebration isn't evidence of a refusal to assimilate. It's evidence of a community confident enough in its American footing to preserve what it loves about its heritage.

The taco truck tells the same story, if we're honest about it. A taco truck is not a foreign invasion; it's one of the most American things imaginable—a small business, launched with modest capital, serving whoever shows up hungry. The food may be Mexican, but the entrepreneurial hustle is pure Ellis Island. We celebrated the same immigrant energy when it arrived in the form of Italian pushcarts and Jewish delis. We simply forget, each time, that we once feared those too.

Even "press one for English"—perhaps the most reliable trigger for assimilation anxiety—doesn't mean what the anxious think it means. That recording exists precisely *because* it's temporary infrastructure for a generation still learning the language. And here the data is unambiguous. Research by Duke University economist Jacob Vigdor, who constructed an assimilation index tracking immigrants over more than a century, found that today's immigrants are actually assimilating at rates comparable to or faster than the European waves we now nostalgize. By the second generation, English fluency is nearly universal. The "press one" prompt is a bridge, not a wall—and like all bridges, it's meant to be crossed.

So why does the anxiety persist against such consistent evidence? Part of the answer is that assimilation is genuinely invisible while it's happening. We notice the festival, the food truck, the unfamiliar language on a phone menu. We don't notice the quiet, cumulative work of a child doing homework in English, a family buying a home, a grandchild who knows Hmong or Spanish only as the language of loving grandparents. Integration is a slow verb, and slowness rarely makes headlines.

But the deeper answer is uncomfortable. The recurring panic over immigrant assimilation has never really been about the facts of assimilation. If it were, the Duke findings—and a century of similar research—would have settled the matter long ago. Instead, each generation reaches for the same worries, dressed in new clothing, aimed at whichever newcomers happen to be arriving. The Germans were too clannish. The Irish too Catholic. The Italians too foreign. The story repeats because the anxiety was never truly a response to evidence in the first place.

That's the hard truth for anyone hoping that better data will calm the recurring fever. We can point to the festivals that prove cultural confidence, the businesses that prove economic drive, the fluency statistics that prove linguistic integration. We can cite the studies until we're hoarse. And still the anxiety will find new targets, because it operates on a different frequency entirely.

After all, fear doesn't listen to facts.

# The Assimilation Myth: What My Central Valley Roots Taught Me About America's Enduring Story

**SAN DIEGO** — Every generation of Americans, it seems, discovers a new wave of immigrants they're certain will never truly become "one of us." The Irish were too Catholic. The Italians too clannish. The Chinese too foreign. Today, the anxiety centers on Latino immigrants, and the refrain is familiar: *They don't assimilate. They don't learn English. They keep to themselves.*

I grew up in the flat farmland outside Fresno, and I can tell you these claims collapse under the weight of both evidence and lived experience.

## The Kitchen Table Test

My neighbor Refugio came to California from Michoacán in the 1980s to pick grapes. He spoke almost no English. His son Danny and I played baseball in a dusty lot behind the packing sheds. Danny spoke flawless, unaccented English, argued about the Dodgers, and eventually became a high school teacher. His daughter—Refugio's granddaughter—is now a pharmacist in Sacramento who blushes when she admits her Spanish is "kind of rusty."

Three generations. One American arc. This is not the exception. **It is the rule**, and the data proves it.

## What the Numbers Actually Say

Consider the persistent claim that immigrants refuse to learn English:

- Research consistently shows that while first-generation immigrants often retain their native language, **the vast majority of their U.S.-born children speak English fluently**, and by the third generation, most families have lost the ancestral language entirely.
- The Pew Research Center has documented that roughly **88 percent of second-generation Latinos** are proficient in English, rising to **94 percent** by the third generation—a trajectory nearly identical to the German, Italian, and Polish waves before them.

On the economic front:

- Second-generation immigrants **surpass the earnings** of their parents and often match or exceed those of comparable native-born Americans.
- Immigrants start businesses at higher rates than the native-born population, seeding Main Streets and strip malls with taquerias, auto shops, and dental practices that anchor local economies.
- In the Central Valley, immigrant labor doesn't just supplement the agricultural economy—**it is the agricultural economy**, generating billions in output that feeds the nation.

Civically, the picture is equally clear:

- Immigrants and their children **serve in the U.S. military** in significant numbers, a form of assimilation that asks for the highest possible price.
- Naturalized citizens **vote, sit on juries, coach Little League, and run for school board**. Latino electoral participation continues to climb with each generation born on American soil.

## Redefining the Terms

The complaint about "assimilation" often smuggles in a hidden demand: that immigrants shed every trace of their origins overnight. But that has never been how America works.

My hometown celebrates its Portuguese heritage with an annual festival featuring a parade and sweet bread. Nobody questions whether the descendants of those dairy farmers are "real" Americans. We eat St. Patrick's Day corned beef and Oktoberfest bratwurst without demanding proof of allegiance. **Cultural retention and American belonging have always coexisted.** The mariachi at a Cinco de Mayo celebration is no more separatist than the bagpipes at a Scottish games.

Assimilation was never about erasure. It was about addition—each group folding its ingredients into a larger recipe.

## The Real Lesson

When I hear someone insist that today's immigrants are different, that *these* newcomers won't blend in, I think of Refugio watching his granddaughter graduate from pharmacy school, wearing the same proud, slightly bewildered expression my own grandfather must have worn generations ago.

The anxiety is old. The outcome is predictable. And the evidence—economic, cultural, and civic—points the same direction it always has: toward a country continually renewed by the people bold enough to join it.

The immigrants are assimilating. They always have. The only question is whether the rest of us will recognize it before history, once again, proves the skeptics wrong.

*— [Columnist Name] writes about California, community, and the American experience.*

Before publication, I'd recommend verifying the specific statistics against the most current reports, as exact percentages shift with new studies and you'll want precise, citable figures for a published piece.

# The Recurring Myth of the Unassimilable Immigrant

Throughout American history, each new wave of immigrants has been greeted by the same anxious refrain: *these* newcomers are different. *These* immigrants won't learn the language, won't adopt our values, won't become truly American. Yet time and again, these fears have proven not just exaggerated but fundamentally wrong. Understanding this pattern—and the evidence that contradicts it—reveals assimilation anxiety as a recurring cultural phenomenon rather than a response to genuine crisis.

## A History of Repeated Alarm

The fear of unassimilable immigrants is remarkably consistent across eras, with only the targeted groups changing. In the 1750s, Benjamin Franklin fretted that German immigrants in Pennsylvania would never adopt English customs, complaining they would "Germanize us instead of our Anglifying them." In the mid-19th century, Irish Catholics faced accusations that their religious loyalties made them incompatible with American democracy. By the early 20th century, the alarm shifted to Italians, Poles, Jews, and other Southern and Eastern Europeans, whom influential voices deemed racially and culturally incapable of integration.

These concerns were not fringe positions. They shaped major policy, culminating in the restrictive Immigration Act of 1924, which established national-origin quotas designed to preserve the country's existing ethnic composition. The intellectual scaffolding for these laws included now-discredited eugenic theories and confident predictions that certain groups would form permanent unassimilated enclaves.

The descendants of those supposedly unassimilable Italians, Poles, and Jews are, of course, now considered unremarkably American. This historical amnesia is telling: the very groups once deemed threats to national cohesion became, within a generation or two, part of the mainstream that expressed anxieties about the *next* wave.

## What the Research Actually Shows

Contemporary scholarship provides compelling evidence that today's immigrants are assimilating—and doing so at rates comparable to or faster than earlier waves.

The most comprehensive recent examination came from the **National Academy of Sciences**, whose 2015 report *The Integration of Immigrants into American Society* concluded that immigrants are integrating well across measures of language, education, occupation, and civic participation. The report found that integration generally increases over time and across generations, following patterns established by earlier immigrant groups.

Perhaps the most striking research comes from economists **Ran Abramitzky and Leah Boustan**, whose work using millions of historical records forms the basis of their book *Streets of Gold*. By tracking immigrants and their children across census records, they found that today's immigrants are assimilating *as quickly as* immigrants of a century ago—and by some measures faster. Their research on names, for instance, shows that immigrants today shed distinctively foreign first names for their children at rates similar to past generations, a marker of cultural integration.

On the crucial question of language, the data is unambiguous. Research consistently shows that while first-generation immigrants often retain their native tongue, their children become bilingual, and by the third generation, English dominance is nearly universal—the same pattern that dissolved German, Italian, and Yiddish-speaking communities of the past. If anything, the pressure toward English is *stronger* today, given its global dominance and pervasiveness in media.

Economic integration tells a similar story. Abramitzky and Boustan found that the children of poor immigrants today achieve upward mobility at rates comparable to the children of poor immigrants in the early 20th century, moving up the economic ladder faster than the children of U.S.-born parents of similar economic backgrounds.

## Why the Fear Persists

If the evidence is so clear, why does assimilation anxiety recur so reliably? Several factors explain the pattern.

First, assimilation is gradual and generational, while its early stages are highly visible. A first-generation immigrant speaking their native language in public is more noticeable than the same family's fully assimilated grandchildren. Observers mistake a snapshot of the integration process for evidence of its failure.

Second, nostalgia distorts memory. Each generation imagines a past era of seamless assimilation that never actually existed—forgetting that yesterday's immigrants faced the identical suspicions now directed at newcomers.

Third, cultural and economic anxieties often find expression through concerns about immigrants, who serve as a convenient focus for broader fears about social change. Assimilation rhetoric frequently reflects unease about a changing society more than any measurable failure of integration.

## Conclusion

The fear that immigrants won't assimilate is one of the most durable and reliably mistaken beliefs in American history. It has been directed at Germans, Irish, Italians, Jews, and countless others—all of whom, contrary to confident predictions, became part of the American mainstream. The research is clear that today's immigrants follow the same trajectory, integrating linguistically, economically, and culturally at rates that match or exceed those of the past.

Recognizing this pattern should inspire not complacency but perspective. When we hear that *this* generation of immigrants is uniquely incapable of becoming American, we would do well to remember that we have heard this exact prediction before—and it has been wrong every single time.
